Guided Inquiry

1 · The force on the rod

The page opens with the rod at rest at x = 0.20 m, with v = 0.20 m/s, R = 0.10 Ω and the field out of the screen. Before pressing Run, predict the direction of the force that the field exerts on the rod once it moves to the right and a current flows in it. Then press Run.

2 · Power in, power out

Keep v = 0.20 m/s and R = 0.10 Ω, with the rod back at rest. Press Run, and press Pause while the rod is about half way along. The readouts show ℰ = 50.0 mV, I = 0.500 A and BIℓ = 125.0 mN. Before looking at the last two readouts, predict how the power the agent supplies in pulling the rod compares with the power that heats the resistor.

3 · The force on one charge

Keep the settings of question 2, with the run paused. The inset shows the marked charge, with its velocity v along +x with the rod and its drift velocity vd along −y down the rod, and their sum as the dashed arrow. Before looking at the bold red arrow, predict the direction of the total magnetic force on the charge relative to its total velocity. Then look.

4 · Pull twice as fast

Now v = 0.40 m/s with R = 0.10 Ω, and the rod is back at rest. Before pressing Run, predict the power the agent must now supply, compared with 25.0 mW at 0.20 m/s. Then press Run.

5 · Double the resistance

Now v = 0.20 m/s again and R = 0.20 Ω, with the rod back at rest. Before pressing Run, predict the power that heats the resistor, compared with 25.0 mW at 0.10 Ω. Then press Run.

6 · Where the energy goes

Pulling the rod at steady speed turns the agent's work into heat: ℰ = Bℓv drives I = ℰ/R, the field pushes back on the rod with BIℓ (Lenz), and the agent's power BIℓv equals I2R.

The magnetic force on each charge is at right angles to its velocity and does no net work; it only passes the agent's energy on to the current. The power, B2ℓ2v2/R, rises as v2 and falls as 1/R.

Pulling a Rod along Rails

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A rod lies across two rails, ℓ = 0.50 m apart and joined at one end through a resistor R, in a uniform field B = 0.50 T out of the screen. The sim pulls the rod along the rails at a steady velocity v and reads out the emf ℰ, the current I, the force BIℓ, the agent's power and the heating.

What you'll learn

  • Where the emf ℰ = Bℓv comes from.
  • Which way the field acts on the rod, and who supplies the power.
  • What the field does to one charge in the rod.
  • How the power depends on v and R.
The set-up seen from above, with the rod a distance x from the resistor.

What's on screen

  • Rails, resistor R and rod, at one fixed scale. The dots ⊙ are B, out of the screen. Markers show ℓ and the distance x of the rod from the resistor.
  • Blue arrows, while the rod moves: the current I round the circuit.
  • Red arrow: the magnetic force BIℓ on the rod.
  • Green arrow: the agent's pull Fagent. Both arrows share a scale on which 250 mN is as long as ℓ.
  • Lower right: the ringed charge q, magnified, with its velocities and the parts of the force on it.
  • Readouts: ℰ and I, then BIℓ, the agent's power Fagentv and the heating I²R.

03

Moving the rod through B drives an emf ℰ = Bℓv

Every charge q in the rod moves with it at v, so the magnetic force of Section 5.1 acts on it: q v × B = −qvB ŷ (notes, eq. 7.10). It lies along the rod and has the same size along the whole length ℓ. The force from the drift of charge along the wires is perpendicular to the wires and adds nothing to the line integral, so the emf comes from the rod alone, with R the total resistance of the circuit (eq. 7.11):

A charge carried along by the rod, with the force on it along the rod.

The force pushes positive charge along −y, so the current circulates clockwise. At the opening values, v = 0.20 m/s and R = 0.10 Ω, ℰ = 50.0 mV and I = 0.500 A.

The flux rule gives the same emf. The flux through the circuit is ΦB = Bℓx and it grows at the rate Bℓv. With the normal along z the positive direction is anticlockwise, so the minus sign in ℰ = −dΦB/dt is a clockwise current (eq. 7.13).

Key idea. The emf Bℓv comes from the magnetic force on the charges that the rod carries along.
See itRun the rod at 0.20 m/s with R = 0.10 Ω and pause it half way. Watch for: ℰ = 50.0 mV and I = 0.500 A, with the blue arrows running clockwise.
04

The field pushes back on the rod with BIℓ, against v

The current I = Bℓv/R runs down the rod, along −y, and a current in a field feels the force Iℓ × B of Section 5.2. With the rod along −ŷ and B along ẑ (notes, eq. 7.23):

The force points along −x, against v, and its size is BIℓ: 125.0 mN at the opening values. This is the sim's Retarding force readout. The minus sign is Lenz's law, and conservation of energy requires it. With the opposite sign a rod given a small push would accelerate without limit while heating the resistor, creating energy from nothing. To keep v steady, the agent pulls with an equal and opposite force, Fagent = BIℓ along +x.

The rod half way along, at x = 0.80 m, with the current, the force on the rod and the agent's pull, as the sim draws them.
Key idea. The field pushes on the current in the rod against v, so the agent must pull with BIℓ.
See itRun the rod at 0.20 m/s with R = 0.10 Ω and pause it half way. Watch for: the red arrow pointing left, against v, the green arrow pointing right, and Retarding force 125.0 mN.
05

The agent's power equals the heating, BIℓv = I²R

The agent does work on the rod at the rate Fagentv = BIℓv. In the notes (eq. 7.24):

This is the rate at which heat is produced in the resistance of the circuit. At the opening values the sim reads Agent's power Fagentv = 25.0 mW and Heating I²R = 25.0 mW, and the two readouts agree at every setting.

The rod keeps the same v, so none of the agent's work goes into its kinetic energy. The rod needs 6.0 s to cross from x = 0.20 m to x = 1.40 m, so the agent does 125.0 mN × 1.20 m = 0.150 J, all of it heat in R.

Key idea. Every joule that heats R was supplied by the agent pulling the rod.
See itPause the running rod and read the two power readouts. Watch for: Agent's power 25.0 mW and Heating 25.0 mW, equal.
06

The total magnetic force on a charge does no work

A magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity of the charge and does no work, yet the circuit receives energy at the rate ℰI. Once the current flows, a charge in the rod has the velocity of the rod, v x̂, and also a drift velocity −vd ŷ along the rod, so the force on it is (notes, eq. 7.12):

Drawn as in the sim's inset: vd enlarged, and the force part it produces enlarged by the same factor.

The scalar product of this force with the total velocity is −qvdvB + qvdvB = 0, so the total force is at right angles to the total velocity and does no work. Its first term pushes the charge along the rod and does work at the rate qvdvB. Its second term pushes the charge against the motion of the rod, so the agent must balance it, doing work at the same rate. The agent therefore supplies the energy, and the magnetic force only redirects it.

Key idea. The two parts of the force do equal and opposite work, and the agent pays for it.
See itPause the running rod and look at the magnified charge in the lower right. Watch for: the bold red arrow F at right angles to the dashed total velocity, between the thin red arrows qvdB (−x) and qvB (−y).
07

The power goes as v² and falls as 1/R

Put ℰ = Bℓv and I = ℰ/R into the results above. The emf goes as v, the current as v/R and the force BIℓ as v/R, and the power B²ℓ²v²/R goes as v² and falls as 1/R.

Doubling v to 0.40 m/s, with R = 0.10 Ω, doubles ℰ, I and BIℓ to 100.0 mV, 1.000 A and 250.0 mN, and the power rises fourfold, from 25.0 mW to 100.0 mW. Doubling R to 0.20 Ω, at 0.20 m/s, leaves ℰ at 50.0 mV, halves I to 0.250 A and BIℓ to 62.5 mN, and halves the power to 12.5 mW. The rod is easier to pull.

The agent's power over the sim's range of v, for its two ends of R.

At 0.40 m/s the rod crosses the rails in 3.0 s instead of 6.0 s, so the energy per run, 0.300 J, only doubles.

Key idea. P = B²ℓ²v²/R: four times the power for twice the v, and half the power for twice the R.
See itPull at 0.40 m/s with R = 0.10 Ω and pause the rod half way. Watch for: Agent's power 100.0 mW, four times 25.0 mW.
See itPull at 0.20 m/s with R = 0.20 Ω and pause the rod half way. Watch for: I = 0.250 A and Heating 12.5 mW, half of 25.0 mW.
08

Summary

In one line. A rod pulled at a steady velocity along rails in a magnetic field acts as a source of emf, and the sim follows the force, power and energy for the rod and for one charge in it.
  • The rod carries charges through B, which gives ℰ = Bℓv and I = Bℓv/R, clockwise (eqs. 7.10, 7.11).
  • The field pushes on the current against v with BIℓ = B²ℓ²v/R, and the agent pulls with the same force (eq. 7.23).
  • The agent's power BIℓv = B²ℓ²v²/R equals the heating I²R (eq. 7.24): 25.0 mW at the opening values.
  • The total magnetic force on a charge does no work, and the agent supplies the energy (eq. 7.12).

Common mix-ups

  • "The field pushes the charges, so it helps the rod along." The force on the current is along −x, against v.
  • "Magnetic forces do no work, so there is no force on the rod." There is a force BIℓ. It is the total force on each charge that does no work.
  • "The field supplies the heat." The agent does, and its power equals I²R.
  • "Twice as fast, half as long on the rails, so the same power." The power rises fourfold, and the energy per run doubles.

Things to try on your own

  • At R = 0.10 Ω, step v from 0.10 to 0.40 m/s and read the agent's power each time.
  • Change only R and check that ℰ stays at 50.0 mV.
